text: AWS Application Load Balancers close a connection that has been idle (no data in either direction) for the idle timeout, 60 seconds by default and configurable from 1 to 4000 seconds. For long operations, AWS advises sending at least 1 byte before each idle period ends and setting the application's own idle timeout above the load balancer's.
why: Hour-long requests through a cloud load balancer fail silently without this.

text: TCP keep-alives are optional in the TCP standard; if implemented they must be off by default, and the interval must default to no less than two hours (RFC 9293). TCP itself has no built-in liveness detection, so applications usually add their own heartbeats.
why: Explains why 'TCP never breaks' also means 'TCP may not notice the peer is gone'.

text: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default: several requests and responses share one connection until someone sends 'Connection: close'. Under HTTP/1.0 the connection stayed open only if the 'keep-alive' option was sent and honored (RFC 9112, section 9.3).
why: Corrects the default the item states.

text: gRPC sends HTTP/2 PING frames as keepalives so a long-lived connection is not treated as idle by proxies or load balancers. On the server, MAX_CONNECTION_IDLE and MAX_CONNECTION_AGE (both infinite by default) can close connections deliberately. Note that AWS Application Load Balancers do not count HTTP/2 PINGs as activity for their idle timeout.
why: Shows what actually keeps gRPC connections alive in production.

text: Go's standard net/http server cancels a request's Context when the client's connection closes, when the request is canceled over HTTP/2, or when the handler returns. A handler that passes this context to its database or downstream calls stops work when the user goes away.
why: A concrete, standard-library way to do what the student asked.

text: Canceling a BigQuery job is not guaranteed: the job may already have finished or be in a stage that cannot be canceled, and you can still be charged depending on when it was canceled. Cancellation usually completes in under a minute.
why: Readers should not assume cancel = no cost.

text: Nginx's default upstream method is weighted round robin: each server has 'weight' (default 1), so a server with weight=5 next to two weight-1 servers gets 5 of every 7 requests.
why: Shows where the weights from the 4 GB/8 GB example are configured.

text: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone for automatic failover, but AWS notes this 'isn't a scaling solution': the standby cannot serve reads. Redundancy (no single point of failure) and scale-out (more capacity) are separate properties.
why: A concrete counter-example to 'not horizontally scalable = SPOF'.

text: Google's SRE book warns that queries per second is a poor capacity unit because the cost of different queries varies and changes as the software changes. It recommends measuring capacity directly in resources; CPU consumption alone works well as the provisioning signal in most cases.
why: Refines what 'requests per server' unit economics should measure.

text: Redis 8.4 added 'DELEX key IFEQ value', which deletes a lock key only if it still holds the caller's random value. This replaces the Lua compare-and-delete script that earlier versions needed.
why: Version-current form of the safe-release fix shown in class.

text: Majority quorums are what buy fault tolerance: a Raft cluster of 5 servers keeps working if 2 fail, but if more fail it stops making progress rather than returning wrong results.
why: Quantifies the availability gained in exchange for throughput.

text: ZooKeeper's leader election recipe: each candidate creates an EPHEMERAL|SEQUENCE znode, and the lowest sequence number is the leader. When the leader fails, its ephemeral znode disappears, and the candidate watching that znode takes over without a 'herd' of all candidates waking up.
why: Concrete mechanism behind 'another node automatically takes its place'.
